paras: The lynching of Bruce Younger took place about midnight on July 26, 1888, at Halifax Court-House, Virginia, when a party of armed horsemen took Younger, a Black man, from the county jail and hanged him from a footbridge. Younger had been arrested that morning, accused of assaulting Mrs. Robert Dodd, a white woman near Meadsville. Virginia papers described it as the first lynching ever carried out in Halifax County, and correspondents there defended it as justified.

According to a South Boston telegram to the Richmond Dispatch, Mrs. Dodd woke about 1 a.m. on the night of July 25-26 to find a man in her bedroom, who fled after a prolonged struggle while her husband was away at a neighbor's. The Dispatch said the man worked for R. C. Dodd and did not complete the assault. The Richmond Daily Times' local correspondent called the charge rape, while a Danville version printed in the Shenandoah Herald said Younger met Mrs. Dodd in the road.

Younger was arrested on the morning of July 26, identified by Mrs. Dodd, and sent to the Halifax jail by a justice of the peace to await the grand jury. By evening a lynching was rumored, and officials, fearing a clash between white and Black residents if they moved him, left him in the jail under a guard of six or seven men pressed into service by Sheriff Moore.

About midnight the horsemen arrived, and the Daily Times correspondent put their number at about one hundred, silent and directed by signals. When the sheriff refused the keys, the armed men cleared the courtyard, posted guards, and broke open the jail. Younger, who according to the Dispatch protested his innocence 'again and again', was gagged and led a few hundred yards to a creek printed as 'Foot's' or 'Toots' Creek.

Given five minutes to pray, he was then led onto a footbridge about twelve feet high with a rope around his neck and urged to confess. The Dispatch reported that he confessed at the last moment, and added the lynchers' claim that they had agreed to return him to jail if he kept denying the charge. The drop did not break his neck, and the men fired their pistols into him; the body hung there until morning, when the Dispatch correspondent saw twenty-five or thirty bullet wounds.

No report of an inquest or of any arrest of the lynchers appears in the coverage, and the Dispatch said the men had made little effort to hide their faces. Mrs. Dodd was reported in critical condition, with rumors of her death that the Daily Times correspondent could not confirm.

The two Richmond accounts, both from local writers, took the lynchers' side. The Dispatch headed its story 'THEY SWUNG HIM' and called the act 'the swift vengeance of an outraged people', adding that Black as well as white residents thought Younger 'met a deserved fate'. The Daily Times ran 'A Human Fiend Taken From Jail and Lynched', and its correspondent wrote that he did not favor 'such work generally' but thought this 'a justifiable case'. The Shenandoah Herald reported that 'Public sentiment endorsed the lynching.'

Outside Virginia, a short Danville wire ran on July 27 and 28 in Washington, Pennsylvania, Georgia, West Virginia and Kentucky papers, stating the assault as fact. Its headlines ranged from 'Judge Lynch Abroad' and 'He Was Hanged at Night' to 'A Ravisher Lynched' and 'A Lynching Bee in Virginia'. Weekly news summaries in Minnesota, Iowa, Wisconsin, Dakota and Idaho reprinted a one-line version into mid-August, and one Nebraska paper printed it under the head 'A Lynching in Dakota'.

Accounts differed on the place of the hanging, a footbridge in local reports and a tree in the wire. The Shenandoah Herald read Younger's partly burned clothing as a sign that the mob first meant to burn him, while the Dispatch correspondent, who saw the body, attributed the scorching to the close fire of the pistols. Every report of his confession came from accounts sympathetic to the lynchers, and the Daily Times correspondent gave it as hearsay.

reader.title: Lynching of Bruce Younger
bases: A band of armed men broke into the Halifax County jail, took out a Black prisoner charged with assaulting a white woman, and hanged and shot him (A5, A12, A3).

Younger was taken from jail over the sheriff's refusal by a party of armed horsemen, put at about one hundred, and hanged and shot for an alleged assault on a white woman, which the papers called 'swift vengeance' and 'a justifiable case' (A5, A12, A19).

The Richmond Dispatch's South Boston telegram, the Daily Times' Halifax Courthouse correspondent and the Danville wire independently agree that Younger was taken from the Halifax jail at night and hanged (A5, A12, A3).

accounts.label: Richmond Dispatch special telegram (South Boston)
accounts.gist: Gives Mrs. Dodd's account of a bedroom attack, the sheriff's makeshift guard overpowered, Younger's repeated protests of innocence, a confession on the bridge under threat of death, and a hanging and shooting at the footbridge; reports the mob's claim that he was to be spared unless he confessed.

accounts.label: Daily Times Halifax Courthouse correspondent
accounts.gist: About one hundred organized, silent horsemen battered down the jail doors because the keys were with the former jailor's wife, gagged Younger, and hanged and shot him at the Toots Creek footbridge after a reported confession.

accounts.label: Danville wire
accounts.gist: Younger committed an assault on Mrs. Robert Dodge, was jailed by a justice to await the grand jury, and was taken by a party of men to a neighboring wood and hanged to a tree.

accounts.label: Shenandoah Herald (Danville dateline)
accounts.gist: Younger met Mrs. Dood in the road and assaulted her; over a hundred men overpowered the jailor and hanged him to a bridge; partly burned clothing was read as a sign the mob first meant to burn him.

framing.detail: The Richmond Dispatch headed it 'THEY SWUNG HIM. A DETERMINED BAND OF HALIFAX COUNTY LYNCHERS' and called the act 'the swift vengeance of an outraged people.'
The Daily Times headlined 'A Human Fiend Taken From Jail and Lynched' and its correspondent judged it 'a justifiable case.'
The Shenandoah Herald headed it 'Brutal Assault Followed by Lynchling', called Younger 'the brute', and said public sentiment endorsed the lynching.
Out-of-state papers ran the Danville wire under heads such as 'Judge Lynch Abroad', 'He Was Hanged at Night', 'A Ravisher Lynched' and 'A Lynching Bee in Virginia', stating the assault as fact.
